heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Problem Background, 1.2 Restatement of the Problem, 1.3 Global Cybersecurity Index)
note: Nine groups over 21 blocks, about 820 cleaned words. 3 defines cybercrime and points at Figure 1, a chart the section never numbers again. 4 names the CFAA, GDPR and Budapest Convention and ends by printing the '1.2 Restatement of the Problem' heading; 5-13 are the task bullets, and 14-15 introduce the GCI as a five-pillar composite index cited to [2], the only concept section in the paper. 16 carries both the 'Fig.2 Our work' caption and Stage I; 17-21 walk Stages II-IV. No abstract survives - pages 1-2 have no text layer - so this chapter opens the paper. The numbering then jumps from 1.3 to 3.3.1: the chapter-3 heading and sections 3.1-3.2 sit on the empty pages 9-10, so nothing between 1.3 and 3.3.1 is in the text layer.

heading: 2.1 Assumptions
note: Three assumptions across four blocks, about 85 words, and all three concern how the data is bucketed, not the model: crimes are counted monthly with imprecise dates averaged across months (22-23), near-identical records are merged into one (23-24), and annual demographic figures are treated as monthly-constant (25). Nothing says why cybercrime counts behave like the count model they are fitted with, how the TimeXer exogenous series are assumed to relate to crime, or that policy effects are identified at all. The last block carries the '2.2 Notations' heading.

heading: 2.2 Notations (TABLE I)
note: Five groups over 12 blocks, about 145 words: TABLE I defines counts (n_it, n_dc|it, n_con|it, n_s|it, n_or|it), two Bernoulli indicators (X_loss|nit, X_sig|nit), two ratios (r_th|it, r_loss|it) and n_eff|it. The symbols are glued to their descriptions and printed in a maths font the extraction turns into stray characters, so several rows read as a bare description with the symbol landing on the next line. Equations (1)-(4), which are what actually define these objects, sit on the empty pages 9-10; the only trace is block 44, which reads back (3) and (4) without ever printing them.

heading: 2.3 Data Collection and Visualization (filtering and monthly reconstruction)
note: Seven groups over 11 blocks, about 930 cleaned words, the densest chapter. 38-39 source the data: ITU GCI 2024, the VERIS framework and VCDB (TABLE II). 40-43 point at Figures 3 and 4, both 2014 charts, and 43 sets the filtering rule: records under 'Confidence: None' are dropped, useless files abandoned. 44 is the only place equations (3) and (4) are described - X_loss and X_sig as Bernoulli draws where 'Confirmed' means loss and 'Never miss' means no loss, with suspected events subtracted - and the mapping is a judgement with no validation behind it. 45-46 read the Canada, Great Britain and India timelines and assert that policy changes moved the counts, a visual argument rather than a test. 47-48 then build the monthly series: the annual discrepancy is divided by 12 and any remainder allocated in the fixed order 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8, 11, 3, 6, 9, 12, which fabricates up to ten counts per country-year and is never checked later.

heading: 3.3 Model III: Demographic Parameters and Prediction (3.3.1 Parameter Selection and Data Preprocess, 3.3.2 Correlation Analysis)
note: Ten groups over 19 blocks, about 1380 cleaned words, under the printed heading '3.3 Model III: Define Correlative Demographic Parameters and Make Prediction Accordingly', which is glued into the tail of block 48 on the data-preprocessing side of the boundary. 50 lists the UNESCO predictors (GDP, enrolment, literacy, internet penetration, cybersecurity-server coverage, public education) and 51 prints TABLE III for India 2019-2023, which puts 8 column headers above 9 numeric columns, and whose 'Network Server' column is frozen at 43.4054 from 2020 onwards, staleness never discussed. 52-56 diagnose a June 2023 outlier in the U.S. and merge 735 near-identical records, a fix chosen after seeing the plot. 57-66 run Pearson, Spearman and Kendall on pooled country-feature pairs: TABLE IV prints six coefficients (0.321, 0.311, 0.249, 0.267, -0.099, -0.289) under five column headers, so one number has no label, and 61 discusses 'internet access (Network penetration)' although no such column exists in any table. 67 drops 'Network Server' as the indicator 'closest to 0', yet TABLE IV gives it 0.267 and education -0.099, so the stated rule would have dropped education instead; literacy is kept although the same paragraph admits large data gaps for the U.S.

heading: TimeXer prediction model (3.3.3, no heading in the text layer)
note: Three groups over five blocks, about 470 cleaned words: a description of the TimeXer architecture cited to [13] - patching, endogenous self-attention, exogenous variate embeddings, cross-attention, learnable global tokens. No hyperparameters, no lookback or horizon, no train/validation split, no loss function, no seeds, and no baseline beyond the exogenous/no-exogenous pair of TABLE VII. 72 is where the endogenous and exogenous variable lists should be defined and is truncated at 'the exogenous variables include'.

heading: Problem 1: Global distribution and high-risk regions (Figures 9-12)
note: Four groups over five blocks, about 280 cleaned words. 73 announces that the thwarted, reported and prosecuted maps are 'Figure 4 and Figure 5' and that high targets are 'illustrated in Figure 9 below'; Figure 5 is not in the text layer at all and the target map is Figure 11. 74-76 read the 2014 and 2020 risk maps and name 'the America, Cannada, India, Australia, England'. 77 compares them with the GCI maps while calling them 'Figure 10' although the caption is Figure 12, offers four supporting countries (China, Russia, Thailand, Turkey) and then concedes that 'many countries don't obey this rule'. The risk index is defined only on the empty page 9: equation (5), n_eff|t = sum_t n_t (1 - n_con|t) / (t_end - t_start) over 2003-2023, risk bands >2.0, 2.0-1.5, 1.5-0.5 and <0.5, and Figure 5's four ratio maps (contamination, discovered, severity, success). None of it reaches the text layer, so the maps cannot be reproduced from the text.

heading: Problem 2: Policy effectiveness by class (Figure 13)
note: Three groups over five blocks, about 485 cleaned words. 78 announces the average year-on-year change per policy class, 79-81 are the three panel labels, 82 reads Figure 13 and reports exactly one quantity - 'greater than 100%' in the first year - before asserting a delayed-then-sustained effect. The three classes A, B and C are named only in passing in 46 ('class C policy' for Canada, 'Class B' for India); their definitions sit on the empty page 10, which prints '3.2 Model II: Define Effective Policies', '3.2.1 Policy Analysis and Classification' - three policy areas (institutional development, cooperation, public education and talent) plus the A/B/C abbreviation paragraph - and '3.2.2 Cybercrime Timeline of Some Countries'. The classes exist, but the taxonomy, the country list and the counts behind the three curves are outside the text layer.

heading: Problem 3: Prediction with TimeXer (Figure 14, TABLE VII)
note: Four groups over four blocks, about 185 cleaned words. 83 sets up the U.S. comparison, 84-85 give Figure 14 and TABLE VII (with exogenous MAE 14.313 and MSE 2.938 against 17.668 and 3.659 without), 86 reads them. The table is internally impossible: MAE 14.313 cannot exceed MSE 2.938 on the same units, since MAE is never below RMSE and RMSE is the square root of MSE. There is no train/test split, no forecast horizon, no repeated run, and 86's claim that exogenous variables 'have a certain degree of impact' rests on one country.

heading: Model Evaluation (unnumbered)
note: Two blocks, about 120 words, and the thinnest evaluation in this batch. Advantage 1 is precision, backed by the TABLE VII comparison; advantage 2 is the de-duplication of near-identical records, which is a preprocessing fix rather than a model property. The two disadvantages are that the policy model is built on counts and only ranks the three classes relatively, and that country characteristics are never combined with specific policies. Neither names the missing pages, the invented monthly allocation, or the unreproducible risk index.

heading: 6 Conclusion and 7 Reference
note: Six groups over seven blocks, about 480 words including the reference list. 89-92 restate the four stages and claim that 'cooperation-focused policies showed the most consistent long-term impact' - a ranking no section computes, since Problem 2 reports only ratios above 100% and never compares the three classes. 93-95 are references [1]-[8] as far as the block runs: a Statista page, the GCI pillar paper, Canadian statutes, the Australian and DoD strategies. Inline [13] for TimeXer has no surviving entry, and the list stops mid-sequence because 95 is followed by the '8. Memo' heading.

heading: 8 Memo: Empirical Insights on Cybersecurity Policy Effectiveness and Predictive Models
note: Five groups over ten blocks, about 435 words. The memo is printed in two columns and the extraction interleaves them line by line, so 100-105 read as alternating fragments ('Establishing a Rigorous A / Feature-Fusion-Based / Statistical System for the / Method for / Predicting cybercrime rates / VCDB Dataset'). Reassembled it has a title (96-98), one background paragraph (99), three panels and a closing claim (104-105): that the U.S. ranked first in the 2020 GCI and also recorded the most cybercrime, and that 'pursuing all three types of policies simultaneously is the most effective way to curb' crime. The body never tests that combination, and 104 dates the dataset to 1971-2023 while section 2.3 works with 2014 and 2020 maps.
